CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches over the past few months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
52-year-old male with newly diagnosed pituitary lesion presenting for neurosurgical consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard. Patient presented to primary care on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches. Headaches began approximately three months ago with gradual onset, initially 3/10 in severity and progressively worsened to 6/10. Headaches are located behind the eyes, described as a dull, nagging ache, worse in the morning, lasting a few hours at a time with nothing that makes them better or worse. Patient denies radiation of pain. Denies associated nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. Recently has noticed bumping into door frames. Denies change in vision on formal questioning, though eyes were last checked in the fall. Workup for headaches included brain MRI with contrast and serology studies, which incidentally discovered the pituitary lesion. Patient tried acetaminophen several times without relief and discontinued.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, weakness, syncope, or nausea. No prior history of headaches. No change in vision or balance on patient's subjective assessment. Visual field testing during examination revealed bitemporal hemianopia.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable. No significant past medical history.

MEDICATIONS
None. Patient denies taking any medications.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient is adopted and unaware of family history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a home. Denies alcohol use, tobacco use, and recreational drug use. Denies past use of all substances.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patient is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent. Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit in upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity and eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

RESULTS
Lab work from 3/3/21 including CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, and CRP are all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH with all other results normal. Brain MRI with contrast from 3/4/21 reveals a well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size with no other abnormalities noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Pituitary adenoma with optic chiasmal compression. Patient is a pleasant 52-year-old male with benign-appearing pituitary adenoma incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches. He is symptomatic with clinical and radiographic evidence of optic chiasmal compression. Surgical intervention via transsphenoidal approach is indicated for excision and decompression of the pituitary fossa. Risks of anesthesia discussed including heart attack, stroke, and death. Surgical risks discussed including infection, need for further surgery, cerebrospinal fluid leak, wound infection, seizure, stroke, permanent neurologic deficits, and death. Patient counseled that vision recovery is possible but not guaranteed. Will refer to ophthalmology for formal visual field testing prior to surgery for baseline comparison. Patient to meet with surgery scheduler to arrange operative date and pre-operative visual field testing. Patient expresses understanding and agreement with surgical plan.
